title: Meeting Charlie Parker at 55th and Michigan in Chicago
summary: Parker, hoboing into Chicago, blows with Goon Gardner's group and reminds Budd he used to peek into George E. Lee's rehearsals as a Kansas City boy.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Beautiful. Now you mentioned something about Bird -- Charlie Parker.

Okay. Well, Charlie Parker -- the first time I met Charlie Parker in person, we were in Chicago. Billy Eckstine had met Charlie Parker before, but I hadn't met Charlie Parker, not, you know -- Charlie Parker knew me, but I didn't know him, and I'll give you a reason why he knew me, because that night when I met him, he told me that he was the little boy that used to play stickball out in front of George E. Lee's mother's house where we used to rehearse, and they would come and look --
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- into the window.
What town was that?

This was in Kansas City, Missouri, and that's Charlie's home town. So anyway, I said that to say this -- I said I didn't know Charlie Parker, and so we went up to 55th and Michigan, on the east side of the street this time --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Yeah. There was a club. I don't remember the name of that little club --
(Simultaneous remarks)
55th and Michigan.
-- on the east side of the street.
On the east side of the street.
Would that be the Golden Lily?
No, the Golden Lily was on Michigan. See -- hey look, you remember Goon's name? You remember Gardner Goon that played, that saxiphone player?
(Unintelligible) McKinley Easton?
I believe that is -- anyway, Goon was playing there and King Kolax Collacks.
No, that wasn't his name, but I remember Goon. But that isn't his name. There was also alto player by the name of McKinley Easton.
Yeah. Well, Goon -- Billy Eckstine would go cram me down my throat if he knew I couldn't remember Goon's name because we were good friends. But

King Kolax anyway, Kane Collacks was working there in his group. They have five pieces. So we were in there to hear him. We sat at the bar drinking, so all of a sudden here walks in this little cat, and he looked like hell. And Billy recognized him, and he said, hey, Charlie. And Charlie came up to the bar. Billy bought him a drink, and then we learned that he had just hoboed into Chicago off of the freight train. And so Billy said, wait a minute. So he walked up to Goon. He says, look, when you come off, he says, when you come off, he says, I want you to let this little cat blow the saxophone.

So Goon don't know who Charlie Parker is, and I don't know who Charlie Parker is, you know, so when they come off at intermission, Goon is very happy to let him get up and blow because, you know, we were always looking for some relief so we could get down and that cat with the chicks and whatnot.
Just let me say this before you finish. Goon -- I remember Goon because he was tall.
That is right, tall --
(Simultaneous remarks)
And he was a beautiful saxophone player.
Beautiful saxophone player.
So he handed Charlie Parker his horn, and Charlie convinced the piano player to stand up there -- stay up on the bandstand and play a couple of numbers with
him. Well, this cat turned a-loose on that horn. I said, what?
(Laughter)

I couldn't believe it. I said, what? So after he played all his horn, he came back down to the bar, and he said, Budd Johnson, you don't remember me, he says, you couldn't remember me because I was just a little cat; when you was around Kansas City, I was the little cat out front playing stick ball on Euclid Avenue in front of George E. Georgia Lee's mother's house where you guys used to rehearse, and I would peep through the window listening to you guys. And Charlie Parker couldn't have been over ten or 11 years old at that time.
And from then on we became good friends.
